goals: Explain how bacteria help to make antibiotics, serums and vaccines
Draw and explain the nitrogen cycle and name the bacteria in each step
Describe the role of bacteria in curing tea and tanning leather

slides.heading: Bacteria that Help Us
slides.body_md: Part 1 — bacteria in medicine, in the soil and in industry.

visual.alt: Flow from bacteria to their uses in medicine, soil fertility and industry

slides.narration: Many people think of bacteria only as germs. But most bacteria are harmless and many are very useful. They give us medicines, keep soil fertile and take part in some industries.

slides.heading: Antibiotics, serums and vaccines

rows: A chemical made by a microbe that stops or kills other microbes
Weakened or killed germs, or their harmless products
Makes the body produce its own antibodies
Liquid from the blood of an immunised animal, rich in ready-made antibodies

visual.alt: Table comparing an antibiotic, a vaccine and a serum by what it is, how it works and an example

slides.narration: An antibiotic is a chemical that kills or stops germs, and some come from bacteria. A vaccine trains the body to make its own antibodies. A serum gives ready made antibodies, so it acts at once but protects only for a short time.

slides.heading: Quick check: a vaccine
slides.narration: Think of how the body learns to fight a germ.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a vaccination drive
slides.body_md: A village has 600 children. A health team vaccinates 450 of them in the first week. What percentage is vaccinated, and how many remain?
bullets: Step 1: remaining = 600 − 450 = **150**.
Step 2: percentage vaccinated = 450 ÷ 600 × 100 = **75 percent**.
Step 3: percentage still to be vaccinated = **25 percent**.

visual.alt: Worked table of a vaccination drive: six hundred children, four hundred and fifty vaccinated and one hundred and fifty left

slides.narration: Subtract the vaccinated children from the total to find how many are left. Then divide the vaccinated number by the total and multiply by one hundred. Four hundred and fifty out of six hundred is seventy five percent.

slides.body_md: Air is about **seventy-eight percent nitrogen**, but plants cannot use nitrogen gas. **Rhizobium** in **root nodules** changes it into a usable form.

slides.narration: Plants need nitrogen to make proteins, but they cannot take up the gas from the air. In the roots of pulse plants, such as gram and pea, live Rhizobium bacteria in small swellings called nodules. They make nitrogen compounds that the plant can use.

slides.heading: The nitrogen cycle
slides.body_md: Nitrogen moves between the **air**, the **soil**, **plants** and **animals**, with bacteria in four of the steps.

slides.narration: Follow the cycle. Nitrogen fixing bacteria turn nitrogen gas into ammonia compounds. Nitrifying bacteria change ammonia into nitrates. Plants absorb nitrates and animals eat plants. Decay bacteria return ammonia from dead remains, and denitrifying bacteria send nitrogen back to the air.

slides.heading: The bacteria of the cycle

rows: Change nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds
Rhizobium (in root nodules); Azotobacter and Clostridium (free in the soil)
Break down dead remains and wastes to release ammonia
Change ammonia to nitrites, and nitrites to nitrates
Change nitrates back to nitrogen gas

visual.alt: Table of the four groups of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle with what they do and examples

slides.narration: Learn the four groups. Fixing bacteria, such as Rhizobium, take nitrogen from the air. Decay bacteria make ammonia. Nitrifying bacteria make nitrates. Denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the air.

slides.heading: Quick check: nitrogen fixing
slides.body_md: Which bacteria live in the root nodules of pulse plants?
slides.narration: Think of gram and pea plants.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: nitrogen in air
slides.body_md: A tank holds 500 litres of air. If air is 78 percent nitrogen, how many litres of nitrogen are there, and how much is other gases?
bullets: Step 1: nitrogen = 78 ÷ 100 × 500 = **390 litres**.
Step 2: other gases = 500 − 390 = **110 litres**.

visual.alt: Worked table of nitrogen and other gases in five hundred litres of air

slides.narration: Find seventy eight percent of five hundred, which is three hundred and ninety litres of nitrogen. The rest of the air, one hundred and ten litres, is oxygen and other gases. Yet plants still cannot use this nitrogen directly.

slides.heading: Quick check: ammonia to nitrate
slides.body_md: Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter are examples of which group of bacteria?
slides.narration: They make nitrates.

slides.heading: Tea and leather

rows: Bacteria act on the dried and rolled leaves during curing
Gives the tea its flavour and aroma
Bacteria act on the soaked hides, loosening hair and fat
The hide becomes soft and flexible leather

visual.alt: Table of the role of bacteria in curing tea and tanning leather

slides.narration: Bacteria also work in industry. In curing tea, they help to give the leaves their flavour. In tanning, bacteria loosen the hair and fat on a hide, so that it can be made into soft, flexible leather.

slides.heading: Quick check: a tannery
slides.body_md: Bacteria help in the tanning of leather by
slides.narration: Think of what must be removed from the hide.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Antibiotics kill germs; vaccines teach the body to make antibodies; serums give ready-made antibodies.
Nitrogen cycle: fixation, decay, nitrification, denitrification.
Rhizobium lives in the root nodules of pulse plants.
Bacteria help in curing tea and tanning leather.

visual.alt: Summary table of the four steps of the nitrogen cycle and the bacteria involved

slides.narration: To recap. Bacteria give us antibiotics, vaccines and serums. They keep the soil fertile through the nitrogen cycle, and they play a part in curing tea and tanning leather.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: A **vaccine** gives **long-lasting** protection; a **serum** gives **quick, short** protection.
Name the **bacteria** at each step of the nitrogen cycle, not just the step.
In a nitrogen cycle diagram, add **arrows** and **labels** on each arrow.
**Nitrification** makes nitrates; **denitrification** returns nitrogen to the air.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Do not mix up a vaccine and a serum. Name the bacteria at each step of the nitrogen cycle. Draw arrows with labels. And remember that nitrification makes nitrates, but denitrification returns nitrogen to the air.

goals: Give examples of harm caused by bacteria and suggest ways to prevent food spoilage
Explain the role of yeast in baking and brewing

slides.heading: Harmful Bacteria and Useful Fungi
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how bacteria spoil food and cause disease, and how fungi help in the kitchen.

visual.alt: Flow from harmful bacteria to prevention to useful fungi

slides.narration: Some bacteria are harmful. They spoil our food and cause disease. We can stop many of them. And some fungi, such as yeast and mushrooms, are very useful to us.

slides.heading: Harm done by bacteria

rows: Cooked rice, milk and meat turn sour or smelly; some bacteria also cause food poisoning
Citrus canker of lemon and orange trees
Spores of the anthrax bacterium have been misused as a weapon

visual.alt: Table of the harm done by bacteria with an example of each

slides.narration: Bacteria spoil food and cause diseases of plants, animals and people. A few dangerous kinds, such as the anthrax bacterium, have been misused as weapons, which is why such weapons are banned.

slides.heading: How fast bacteria multiply
slides.body_md: In a warm kitchen, bacteria in cooked rice can **double every thirty minutes**.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: bacteria in rice
slides.body_md: Cooked rice has 100 bacteria. They double every 30 minutes. How many are there after 180 minutes (three hours)?
bullets: Step 1: number of doublings = 180 ÷ 30 = **6**.
Step 2: bacteria = 100 × 2 six times = 100 × 64 = **6400**.

visual.alt: Worked table of bacteria in rice at zero, sixty, one hundred and twenty and one hundred and eighty minutes

slides.narration: First count how many times the bacteria can double in the time. Three hours is one hundred and eighty minutes, which is six doublings. Multiply one hundred by sixty four. The answer is six thousand four hundred bacteria.

slides.heading: Preventing food spoilage

rows: Low temperature slows the growth of bacteria
Kills germs and keeps new ones out
Draws water out of bacteria or makes the food too sour for them

visual.alt: Table of five methods of preventing food spoilage with the reason each works and what it is used for

slides.narration: Bacteria need warmth, water and food. Each method takes away one of these or kills the bacteria. Cold slows them. Heat kills them. Salt, sugar, vinegar and drying take away the water or make the food unsuitable.

slides.narration: Salt and oil are used.

sections.heading: 1. Useful bacteria in medicine: antibiotics, serums and vaccines
sections.body_md:
Most bacteria are harmless and many are useful. In medicine:

| Product | What it is | How it protects | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Antibiotic** | A chemical made by a microbe that **kills or stops the growth** of other microbes | Attacks disease-causing bacteria | **Streptomycin**, made by the bacterium **Streptomyces** |
| **Vaccine** | **Weakened or killed germs**, or their harmless products | The body makes its **own antibodies** and remembers the germ: **long-lasting** protection | Vaccines against typhoid, tetanus |
| **Serum** | Liquid from the blood of an **immunised animal** (for example a horse), rich in **ready-made antibodies** | **Immediate** but **short-lived** protection | Anti-snake-venom serum, anti-tetanus serum |

A vaccine is given **before** infection to prevent a disease; a serum is given **after** a bite or infection when quick help is needed.

key_terms.definition_md: A chemical produced by a microbe that kills or stops the growth of other microbes.
A preparation of weakened or killed germs that makes the body produce antibodies.
Blood liquid of an immunised animal containing ready-made antibodies.

sections.heading: 2. Bacteria in agriculture: the nitrogen cycle
sections.body_md:
Air is about **78 percent nitrogen** by volume, but plants **cannot use nitrogen gas**. They take up **nitrates** from the soil and use them to make proteins. Bacteria move nitrogen round in a **cycle**:

1. **Nitrogen fixation:** nitrogen gas to nitrogen compounds (ammonia) by **nitrogen-fixing bacteria**: **Rhizobium** (in the **root nodules** of pulse plants such as gram, pea and groundnut) and **Azotobacter**, **Clostridium** (free in the soil). Lightning also makes some nitrates (not bacteria).
2. **Nitrification:** ammonia to nitrites by **Nitrosomonas**, then nitrites to **nitrates** by **Nitrobacter**.
3. **Absorption:** plants take up nitrates and make proteins; animals eat the plants.
4. **Decay (ammonification):** **decay bacteria** break down proteins in dead remains and wastes and release **ammonia**.
5. **Denitrification:** **Pseudomonas** (and similar bacteria) change nitrates back to **nitrogen gas**, which returns to the air.

Growing a pulse crop makes the soil richer in nitrogen compounds; denitrification is often faster in waterlogged soil and lowers fertility.

**Diagram:** draw the cycle with the air, the soil (ammonia, nitrates), plants and animals, dead remains, and the arrows labelled with the process and the bacteria.

Conversion of ammonia to nitrites and then nitrates by nitrifying bacteria.

sections.heading: 3. Bacteria in industry: curing of tea and tanning of leather
sections.body_md:
- **Curing tea:** tea leaves are dried, rolled and kept for some time. **Bacteria** act on the leaves and help to give the tea its **flavour and aroma**.
- **Tanning leather:** animal hides are soaked in vats. **Bacteria** act on the hides, **loosening the hair and fat** and helping to make the hide **soft and flexible**. Chemical tanning then makes it into leather.

key_terms.definition_md: Treating tea leaves, with the help of bacteria, to develop flavour and aroma.
Converting animal hides into leather; bacteria help to soften the hide and loosen hair.

sections.heading: 4. Harmful bacteria: food spoilage, diseases, bio-weapons
sections.body_md:
| Harm | Example |
|---|---|
| **Food spoilage** | Cooked rice, milk and meat turn sour or smelly; some bacteria cause **food poisoning** |
| **Diseases of plants** | Citrus canker of lemon and orange |
| **Diseases of humans and animals** | Cholera, typhoid, tuberculosis, tetanus, anthrax |
| **Bio-weapons** | Spores of the anthrax bacterium have been misused as a weapon; such weapons are banned |

Bacteria multiply fast by dividing: in warm food they may **double every 20 to 30 minutes**.

**Preventing food spoilage:** **refrigeration** (cold slows growth); **boiling or pasteurisation** (heat kills); **canning** (heat and sealing); **salting**, **adding sugar or vinegar** (draw out water or make the food too sour); **drying** (no water). Cleanliness in the kitchen also helps.

key_terms.definition_md: Change in food caused by microbes that makes it unfit to eat.
Heating milk to a fixed temperature for a short time to kill bacteria.
Disease-causing microbes misused as a weapon.

sections.heading: 5. Useful fungi: breweries, bakeries, cheese and mushrooms
sections.body_md:
- **Yeast** is a **single-celled fungus** that multiplies by **budding**. It breaks down sugar **without oxygen** (fermentation): glucose gives **alcohol** and **carbon dioxide**.
  - **Bakery:** the **carbon dioxide** makes bubbles in the dough, which **rises**; the alcohol evaporates during baking.
  - **Brewery:** yeast turns the sugar of grain or grape juice into **alcohol** (beer, wine).
- **Cheese:** **moulds** growing in the curd **ripen** it and give blue cheese and other cheeses their **flavour and texture**.
- **Edible mushrooms** are **fungi** (no chlorophyll). They are grown on compost in trays and are rich in **protein** and low in fat. Some wild mushrooms are **poisonous**.

The industrial manufacture of products with fungi is **not** part of this course.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up a **vaccine** (own antibodies, long-lasting) and a **serum** (ready-made antibodies, quick and short-lived).
- Writing "nitrogen fixation" without naming the **bacteria** or the **root nodules**.
- Saying that **nitrifying** bacteria return nitrogen to the air; that is **denitrification**.
- Writing oxygen for the gas that makes dough rise: it is **carbon dioxide**.
- Calling a mushroom a plant: it is a **fungus**.
- Giving a method of food preservation without the **reason**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a reason.
- 2 marks: two differences or two uses matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a neat flow chart or labelled diagram, or three points with reasons.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation with parts of 2 to 4 marks; one part is usually a labelled diagram or flow chart.

questions.stem_md: A farmer grows groundnut in a field after a wheat crop. The next wheat crop grows better, mainly because the groundnut plants

options.text_md: kill all the bacteria in the soil
leave nitrogen compounds in the soil through Rhizobium in their roots

questions.solution_md: Rhizobium in the root nodules of groundnut fixes nitrogen and enriches the soil — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Pulse crops make the soil richer in nitrogen compounds.

**Reason (R):** Rhizobium in the root nodules changes nitrates into nitrogen gas.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: Rhizobium changes nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Nitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas from the soil to the air.
questions.solution_md: False. Nitrifying bacteria make nitrates; denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the air.

questions.stem_md: Rhizobium bacteria live inside swellings on the roots of pulse plants called root ______.
questions.solution_md: Nodules.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Clostridium, Nitrosomonas.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nitrosomonas**; the others are **nitrogen-fixing bacteria**.

questions.solution_md: Nitrosomonas is a nitrifying bacterium.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: farmers grow pulses in rotation with cereals.

answer.model_answer_md: **Rhizobium** in the root nodules of pulses **fixes nitrogen** and **enriches the soil** with nitrogen compounds.

questions.solution_md: Rhizobium fixes nitrogen.

questions.stem_md: Air is 78 percent nitrogen by volume. How many litres of nitrogen are there in 2000 litres of air?
What is nitrification? Name the two bacteria that bring it about.

answer.model_answer_md: **Nitrification** is the change of **ammonia** into **nitrites** and then into **nitrates** in the soil. It is brought about by **Nitrosomonas** (ammonia to nitrite) and **Nitrobacter** (nitrite to nitrate).

questions.solution_md: Ammonia to nitrates; Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter.

questions.stem_md: Name one nitrogen-fixing bacterium that lives in root nodules and one that lives freely in the soil.

answer.model_answer_md: In the root nodules of pulse plants the bacterium is **Rhizobium**. A bacterium living freely in the soil is **Azotobacter** (or **Clostridium**). Both change nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds.

questions.solution_md: Rhizobium; Azotobacter.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between nitrifying bacteria and denitrifying bacteria.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Nitrifying bacteria | Denitrifying bacteria |
|---|---|
| Change **ammonia into nitrates** | Change **nitrates into nitrogen gas** |
| Examples: **Nitrosomonas**, **Nitrobacter** | Example: **Pseudomonas** |
| **Increase** the nitrates available to plants | **Reduce** the nitrates, lowering soil fertility |
| Active in well-aerated soil | Active mainly in waterlogged soil |

questions.solution_md: Change brought about; examples; effect on fertility.

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the root system of a pulse plant showing the root nodules. Label the main root, a lateral root and a root nodule.

answer.model_answer_md: A **main root** running down from the soil level, with **lateral roots** branching off it; small round **root nodules** on the lateral roots, and the nodules enlarged to show **Rhizobium**. Three labels with ruled lines.

questions.solution_md: Root system with nodules; three labels.

Select the correct terms to fill in the blanks: [nitrates, ammonia, nitrogen, Rhizobium, nodules, denitrification, nitrification, antibiotic]

Plants cannot use (a) ______ gas from the air. In pulse plants the bacterium (b) ______ lives in root (c) ______. Nitrifying bacteria change (d) ______ to nitrates, and the return of nitrogen to the air is called (e) ______.
questions.solution_md: (a) nitrogen; (b) Rhizobium; (c) nodules; (d) ammonia; (e) denitrification.

questions.solution_md: A nitrogen fixation: Rhizobium and Azotobacter; B decay: decay bacteria; C nitrification: Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter; D denitrification: Pseudomonas; E absorption: root hairs.

questions.stem_md: A tea taster says that the flavour and aroma of a cup of tea partly come from changes made in the leaves during curing. These changes are helped by
questions.solution_md: Bacteria act on the leaves during curing and give flavour and aroma — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Animal hides are soaked in large vats for several days before being made into leather. Bacteria in the vats help by

options.text_md: loosening the hair and fat of the hide
making the hide stronger and thicker
killing the other bacteria in the vat

questions.solution_md: Bacterial action loosens the hair and fat so that the hide becomes soft — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the process in which bacteria act on dried tea leaves to develop their flavour and aroma.

answer.model_answer_md: **Curing** (of tea leaves).

questions.solution_md: Curing.

questions.stem_md: State the role of bacteria in the curing of tea leaves. What quality do they give to the tea?

answer.model_answer_md: Bacteria **act on the dried, rolled tea leaves** during curing. They give the tea its **flavour and aroma**.

questions.solution_md: Act on leaves; flavour and aroma.

questions.stem_md: Explain how bacteria help in the tanning of leather.

answer.model_answer_md: The hides are **soaked in vats**, where **bacteria loosen the hair and fat** on them. The hide then becomes **soft and flexible** and can be made into leather.

questions.solution_md: Loosen hair and fat; soft hide.

questions.stem_md: Describe the role of bacteria in (i) curing tea and (ii) tanning leather.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Curing tea:** bacteria act on the dried and rolled leaves and give the tea its **flavour and aroma**.
(ii) **Tanning:** the hides are soaked in vats and the bacteria **loosen the hair and fat**; the hide becomes **soft and flexible** leather.

questions.solution_md: Tea: flavour and aroma. Tanning: loosen hair and fat; soft leather.

questions.stem_md: Spores of a certain bacterium that causes a serious disease of cattle and humans have been misused as a weapon in some countries. The bacterium causes
questions.solution_md: Anthrax spores have been misused as a bio-weapon — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The leaves and fruits of a lemon tree show raised, brown, corky spots. The disease, called citrus canker, is caused by
questions.solution_md: Citrus canker is a bacterial disease of plants — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A jar of jam containing a very high amount of sugar stays fresh for a long time, because the sugar

options.text_md: draws water out of bacteria and so stops their growth

questions.solution_md: A strong sugar solution draws water out of bacterial cells — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Packet milk that has been heated to a fixed temperature for a short time stays fresh longer than raw milk, because heating

options.text_md: removes the water from the milk
kills most of the bacteria in the milk

questions.solution_md: Pasteurisation kills the bacteria that spoil milk — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A few hours after eating stale cooked meat at a picnic, several children have vomiting and stomach pain. The most likely cause is

options.text_md: too much oxygen in the meat
bacteria that multiplied in the meat
lack of sunlight on the meat
a lack of salt in the meat

questions.solution_md: Bacteria that grow in stale food can cause food poisoning — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Food kept in a refrigerator stays fresh longer.

**Reason (R):** Low temperature slows the growth of bacteria.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and slow bacterial growth explains why food lasts longer — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? All bacteria are harmful to humans.
questions.solution_md: False. Many bacteria are useful: they make antibiotics and vaccines, fix nitrogen and help in tanning and curing tea.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: pickles and jams do not spoil easily.

answer.model_answer_md: **Salt, vinegar or sugar** draw water out of bacteria or make the food unsuitable, so **bacteria cannot grow**.

questions.solution_md: Bacteria cannot grow.

questions.stem_md: A sample of milk contains 250 bacteria. They double every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are there after 60 minutes?
questions.solution_md: Number of doublings $= 60 \div 20 = 3$; bacteria $= 250 \times 2^{3} = 2000$.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by a bio-weapon? Name one bacterium that has been misused in this way.

answer.model_answer_md: A **bio-weapon** is a **disease-causing microbe**, or its toxin, misused to harm people, animals or crops. Example: the **anthrax bacterium** (its spores).

questions.solution_md: Disease-causing microbe misused; anthrax.

questions.stem_md: Name two ways of preventing the spoilage of food by bacteria and state the reason each works.

answer.model_answer_md: **Refrigeration**: low temperature slows the growth of bacteria. **Boiling or canning**: heat kills the bacteria. (**Salting, sugar, vinegar** or **drying** also stop growth by removing water.)

questions.solution_md: Two methods with reasons.

questions.stem_md: Give three ways in which bacteria are harmful to us. Name an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Spoil food**: cooked rice, milk and meat turn sour; some cause food poisoning.
2. **Cause diseases of plants**: citrus canker of lemon.
3. **Cause diseases of humans and animals**: cholera, typhoid, tuberculosis, tetanus or anthrax. (Some, such as anthrax, have been misused as **bio-weapons**.)

questions.solution_md: Spoilage; plant disease; human and animal disease, each with an example.

questions.stem_md: Name three methods of preventing food spoilage and state the principle of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Refrigeration**: low temperature slows the growth of bacteria.
2. **Boiling, pasteurisation or canning**: heat kills the bacteria (and canning keeps new ones out).
3. **Salting, adding sugar or vinegar, or drying**: these remove water or make the food too sour, so bacteria cannot grow.

questions.solution_md: Cold slows growth; heat kills; removing water or making food sour stops growth.

options.text_md: living yeast breaks down sugar and gives off carbon dioxide
living yeast makes the dough colder
boiled yeast turns the sugar to starch

questions.solution_md: Living yeast ferments the sugar and releases carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Sweet grape juice is kept in a closed vessel with yeast for some days. It loses its sweetness and a gas escapes. The new liquid contains
questions.solution_md: Yeast breaks down the sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Under a microscope, a student sees tiny oval cells with small outgrowths in a sugar solution. The cells are multiplying by
questions.solution_md: Yeast cells form small buds that separate to become new cells — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The blue-green veins seen in some ripened cheeses are caused by
questions.solution_md: Moulds growing in the curd ripen the cheese and give the veins — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student says that a mushroom is a plant because it grows in the soil. This is wrong because a mushroom

options.text_md: has no chlorophyll and takes in food from compost

questions.solution_md: A mushroom is a fungus: no chlorophyll, and it absorbs food — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Dough rises because yeast gives off oxygen.

**Reason (R):** Yeast breaks down sugar and releases carbon dioxide.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: the gas is carbon dioxide, not oxygen. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Mushrooms are classified as fungi.

**Reason (R):** Mushrooms have no chlorophyll and absorb their food.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the lack of chlorophyll with absorbed food explains why they are fungi — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Yeast is a single-celled fungus that multiplies by budding.
questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A mushroom is a green plant that makes food by photosynthesis.
questions.solution_md: False. A mushroom is a fungus with no chlorophyll.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Yeast, Mushroom, Mould, Rhizobium.

answer.model_answer_md: **Rhizobium**; the others are **fungi**.

questions.solution_md: Rhizobium is a bacterium.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: bread dough rises when yeast is added to it.

answer.model_answer_md: Yeast breaks down the **sugar** in the dough and releases **carbon dioxide**, which forms bubbles and **raises** the dough.

questions.solution_md: Carbon dioxide from sugar.

questions.stem_md: 5 yeast cells in a sugar solution double in number 3 times by budding. How many cells are there at the end?
Explain why yeast is used in a bakery.

answer.model_answer_md: Yeast **breaks down the sugar** in the dough and releases **carbon dioxide**. The gas forms **bubbles** that make the dough **rise**, so the bread becomes soft and spongy.

questions.solution_md: Carbon dioxide; dough rises.

questions.stem_md: State one use of a fungus in cheese making and one use of mushrooms as food.

answer.model_answer_md: **Moulds** growing in the curd **ripen** the cheese and give it its **flavour and texture**. **Edible mushrooms** are grown on compost and eaten as a food **rich in protein** and low in fat.

questions.solution_md: Moulds ripen cheese; mushrooms are protein-rich food.

questions.stem_md: Explain the role of yeast in (i) a bakery and (ii) a brewery.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Bakery:** yeast breaks down the sugar in the dough and releases **carbon dioxide**; the bubbles make the dough **rise**.
(ii) **Brewery:** yeast breaks down the sugar of grain or grape juice **without oxygen** into **alcohol** and carbon dioxide, giving beer or wine.

questions.solution_md: Bakery: carbon dioxide raises the dough. Brewery: alcohol from sugar.

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of an edible mushroom. Label the cap, stalk and mycelium.

answer.model_answer_md: A **cap** on a **stalk** above the soil level, with **gills** under the cap; below the soil a network of fine threads, the **mycelium**. Three labels with ruled lines.

questions.solution_md: Mushroom with cap, stalk and mycelium.

questions.stem_md:
A farmer grows groundnut in a field after a wheat crop. A student uproots a groundnut plant and sees small swellings on its roots. The student reads that air is 78 percent nitrogen.

(a) Name the swellings and the bacteria that live in them. [2]

(b) Explain why the groundnut plant cannot use the nitrogen of the air directly, although it is so plentiful. [2]

(c) Name the process that returns nitrogen gas to the air and the bacterium that carries it out. [2]

(d) Draw a neat flow chart of the nitrogen cycle, showing nitrogen in air, ammonia, nitrates, plants and animals, with the name of the process on each arrow. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The swellings are **root nodules**; they contain **Rhizobium** bacteria.

**(b)** Plants can take up only **nitrogen compounds such as nitrates**, not nitrogen gas. Rhizobium (nitrogen fixation) must first change the gas into a usable form.

**(c)** **Denitrification**, carried out by **Pseudomonas**.

**(d)** Nitrogen in air → (**nitrogen fixation**, Rhizobium) → ammonia compounds → (**nitrification**, Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter) → nitrates → (**absorption**) → plants → animals; dead remains → (**decay**) → ammonia; nitrates → (**denitrification**) → air.

questions.solution_md: Root nodules with Rhizobium; only nitrates usable; denitrification by Pseudomonas; flow chart of the cycle.

marking_scheme.step: Plants take up only nitrogen compounds

questions.stem_md:
A health team visits a village with 600 children and vaccinates 450 of them in a week. Later a girl in the village is bitten by a venomous snake.

(a) Calculate the number of children not yet vaccinated and the percentage who have been vaccinated. [2]

(b) What is a vaccine? State how it protects a child. [3]

(c) Explain why the girl is given a serum and not a vaccine. [2]

(d) Draw a neat flow chart of the steps by which a vaccine gives protection against a disease. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Not yet vaccinated = 600 − 450 = **150**; percentage vaccinated = 450 ÷ 600 × 100 = **75 percent**.

**(b)** A **vaccine** is a preparation of **weakened or killed germs** (or their harmless products). It makes the body produce **antibodies** against the germ and **remember** it, so the child is protected for a **long time**.

**(c)** A serum contains **ready-made antibodies** that act **at once**; the girl needs quick help, and a vaccine would take too long to make the body produce antibodies.

**(d)** Vaccine (weakened germs) injected → body detects the germ → body makes **antibodies** → body remembers → **protected** if the real germ enters later.

questions.solution_md: 150 children and 75 percent; weakened germs make antibodies; serum acts at once; flow chart.

marking_scheme.step: Acts at once, vaccine is slow
Flow chart of three or more steps in order

questions.stem_md:
A tea estate sends cured leaves to a packing unit, and a tannery in the same town has 4 vats with 15 hides in each. After soaking, 20 percent of all the hides need to be soaked again.

(a) State the role of bacteria in the curing of tea leaves. [2]

(b) State the role of bacteria in the tanning of leather. [2]

(c) Calculate the number of hides in the tannery, the number to be soaked again and the number that are ready. [3]

(d) Draw a neat flow chart showing the steps from a fresh hide to leather. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Bacteria **act on the dried, rolled leaves** and give the tea its **flavour and aroma**.

**(b)** Bacteria in the vats **loosen the hair and fat** on the hide, making it **soft and flexible**.

**(c)** Hides = 4 × 15 = **60**; soaked again = 20 ÷ 100 × 60 = **12**; ready = 60 − 12 = **48**.

**(d)** Fresh hide → soaked in vats → **bacteria loosen hair and fat** → hide made soft and flexible → **tanned** → leather.

questions.solution_md: Flavour and aroma; hair and fat loosened; 60, 12, 48; flow chart.

questions.stem_md:
A cook leaves a pan of milk on a warm table. The milk starts with 250 bacteria, and they double every 20 minutes.

(a) Calculate the number of bacteria after one hour and after two hours. [3]

(b) Explain why the milk would stay fresh for longer in a refrigerator. [2]

(c) Name three methods of preventing food spoilage and state the principle of each. [3]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled bar graph of the number of bacteria at 0, 20, 40 and 60 minutes. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** After one hour: 250 × 2 three times = **2000**. After two hours there are six doublings: 250 × 64 = **16000**.

**(b)** The **low temperature slows** the growth and division of bacteria, so they multiply far more **slowly**.

**(c)** **Refrigeration**: cold slows growth. **Boiling or pasteurisation**: heat kills bacteria. **Salting, sugar, vinegar or drying**: remove water or make the food unsuitable.

**(d)** Time (minutes) on the x-axis and number of bacteria on the y-axis, with four bars: 250, 500, 1000, 2000. Both axes labelled.

questions.solution_md: 2000 and 16000; cold slows growth; three methods; bar graph.

marking_scheme.step: Bars of correct heights with axes labelled

questions.stem_md:
A baker mixes flour, sugar, warm water and yeast. The dough is 500 mL at the start and 1100 mL after two hours in a warm place.

(a) Calculate the percentage increase in the volume of the dough. [2]

(b) Name the gas that makes the dough rise and explain how it is produced. [3]

(c) State what yeast does to grape juice in a brewery and name the two products. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a yeast cell forming a bud. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Gain = 1100 − 500 = 600 mL; percentage increase = 600 ÷ 500 × 100 = **120 percent**.

**(b)** **Carbon dioxide**. Yeast **breaks down the sugar** in the dough and releases the gas, which forms **bubbles** that make the dough **rise**.

**(c)** Yeast breaks down the sugar **without oxygen** (fermentation) into **alcohol** and **carbon dioxide**.

**(d)** A **cell** with a **cell wall**, **nucleus** and **vacuole**, and a small **bud** growing from it. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: 120 percent; carbon dioxide from sugar; alcohol and carbon dioxide; labelled budding yeast.

questions.stem_md:
A mushroom farm has 3 trays of compost. Every tray gives 12 mushrooms at each picking, and the farmer picks 2 times.

(a) Calculate the number of mushrooms picked at one picking and in all. [2]

(b) Give two reasons why a mushroom is classified as a fungus and not as a plant. [2]

(c) State one use of a fungus in cheese making. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a mushroom, naming the cap, gills, stalk and mycelium. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** One picking = 3 × 12 = **36**; in all = 36 × 2 = **72**.

**(b)** It has **no chlorophyll**, so it cannot make food by photosynthesis; it **absorbs food** from the compost; it has a body of thread-like **hyphae** (mycelium) and no true roots, stem and leaves.

**(c)** **Moulds** growing in the curd **ripen** the cheese and give it its flavour and texture (blue cheese).

**(d)** A **cap** with **gills** underneath, a **stalk** above the soil and a network of **mycelium** below it. Four labels with ruled lines.

questions.solution_md: 36 and 72; no chlorophyll, absorbs food; moulds ripen cheese; labelled mushroom.

marking_scheme.step: Mushroom outline with cap and stalk

questions.stem_md:
Study the diagram of the nitrogen cycle, in which five processes are lettered A to E. A farmer finds that a flooded field has lost much of its nitrogen.

(a) Name the processes A, C and D. [3]

(b) Name one symbiotic and one free-living bacterium that carry out process A. [2]

(c) Which process, lettered in the diagram, has become faster in the flooded field? Explain why the field has lost fertility. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the root of a pulse plant showing the root nodules and the bacteria in them. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A: **nitrogen fixation**; C: **nitrification**; D: **denitrification**.

**(b)** Symbiotic: **Rhizobium** (in root nodules); free-living: **Azotobacter** (or Clostridium).

**(c)** **D, denitrification**. Denitrifying bacteria change the **nitrates** in the waterlogged soil into **nitrogen gas**, which escapes to the air, so the soil has **fewer nitrates** for the plants.

**(d)** A **main root** with **lateral roots**; **nodules** on the lateral roots; one nodule enlarged to show **Rhizobium**. Labels.

questions.solution_md: Fixation, nitrification, denitrification; Rhizobium and Azotobacter; denitrification removes nitrates; labelled root with nodules.

marking_scheme.step: Nitrates change to nitrogen gas, so fewer nitrates
